transcription.notes: The Blitz is a mixed-subject test (physics, mathematics, chemistry, informatics — the answer key labels each item, e.g. phys(1), math(1), chem(1), info(1)); 80 numbered items № 1–№ 80, no points printed. Multiple-choice options are printed as unlabelled radio buttons / checkboxes; they are transcribed as a bulleted list in printed order. The answer key refers to them by letters A, B, C, … in that order (for № 12 the options are the numbers 1–4 and the key prints 4; for № 34 the letters ABFG refer to the structures numbered 1, 2, 6, 7). Program listings (№ 10, 24, 59, 65, 76) are printed in a monospace box; they are transcribed as display math with \texttt lines (braces and << cannot appear in prose); indentation rendered with \quad. № 24 prints "int l = 0, r = n – 1" without a semicolon — kept as printed. The recurring italic note prints the non-word „numerсial“ (with a Cyrillic с in the text layer) in 12 problems; fixed to „numerical“ and recorded in tx.edits. Kept as printed (acceptable or grammatical issues not fixed under D-P28): „How many nodes has the tree have?“ (№ 29, grammar), „The voltmeter … show a reading“ (№ 78, agreement error: show → shows, kept as printed), „3 secundum“ (№ 64, Latin word used for seconds), „mols“ (№ 56), „same amount bits“ (№ 66), „block of size even“ (№ 57), „most minimal“ (№ 55), „which names are“ (№ 79), opening quotes ”hot” / ”warm” (№ 58). Chemical formulas are typeset in math italic in the source ($AgNO_3$, $BaSO_4$ …) and kept so; decimal separators kept as printed (0,6 m in № 64; 28,9% in № 52; −0,403 V in № 49; 12,5 in the key for № 42). № 80: the last table row prints „Density of jet A-1 fuel“ with „0.800 g/mL“ spanning the last two columns; transcribed in the second column. The table also has an empty printed row, kept. Answers come from the answer key (solutions page 1), which prints intervals for numeric items; numeric answers use the midpoint with a half-width tolerance and the printed interval in answer.note. № 80 key prints „[0.155;0.2]“, identical to № 78 and implausible for kg of CO2 per passenger — kept as printed and flagged. Text-layer check: every fi/fl/ffi ligature of this PDF is broken in the text layer (fi → X or :, ffi → U, fl → f), e.g. „satisXes“, „Xltered“, „coeUcient“, „fows“, „fights“ for flights, „:rst“; the pages print the correct words, which are kept (tx.disputed).

problems.statement:
Quicksort algorithm that sorts elements at $lo$ through $hi$ (inclusive) of an array $A$ can be expressed as

$$\begin{array}{l}\texttt{algorithm quicksort(A, lo, hi) is}\\ \quad \texttt{if lo < hi then}\\ \qquad \texttt{p := partition(A, lo, hi)}\\ \qquad \texttt{quicksort(A, lo, p - 1)}\\ \qquad \texttt{quicksort(A, p + 1, hi)}\\ \texttt{ }\\ \texttt{algorithm partition(A, lo, hi) is}\\ \quad \texttt{pivot := A[hi]}\\ \quad \texttt{i := lo}\\ \quad \texttt{for j := lo to hi - 1 do}\\ \qquad \texttt{if A[j] < pivot then}\\ \qquad\quad \texttt{swap A[i] with A[j]}\\ \qquad\quad \texttt{i := i + 1}\\ \quad \texttt{swap A[i] with A[hi]}\\ \quad \texttt{return i}\end{array}$$

The letters of the word OLYMPIAD are placed in a random order. How many comparisons in the partition algorithm does the quicksort algorithm need in the worst case to bring the letters back into the correct order?
